blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A parameter is a numerical characteristic of a population: fixed and usually unknown. A statistic is a numerical characteristic computed from a sample: known, and different from one sample to the next.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Once you study a sample instead of the population, you need two names: the true number you want but cannot see (the parameter), and the number you can calculate from the data in front of you (the statistic). By convention, parameters get Greek letters (μ for a population mean, σ for a population standard deviation) and statistics get Roman letters or a “hat” (x̄, s, p̂). The population proportion is the usual exception: some texts write it π, but this book, like many, writes it p, with p̂ for the sample proportion, because π is also the constant 3.14….

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: The true mean birthweight of every newborn in Raipur district this year is a parameter, μ. No one knows it exactly, because no one has weighed every newborn. The mean computed from 200 newborns you measured is a statistic, x̄. A different 200 newborns would give a slightly different x̄, but there is only one μ.

points.html: Parameter: describes the population; fixed; usually unknown; Greek letters (μ, σ), except the proportion, p in this book.
Statistic: computed from a sample; known; varies from sample to sample; Roman letters or hats (x̄, s, p̂).
Statistics estimate parameters. Estimation (Chapter 7) and hypothesis testing (Chapter 8) quantify how far a statistic can be trusted as a stand-in for its parameter.
The sample-to-sample variability of a statistic is formalised as its sampling distribution (§6.5).

blocks.label: Checkpoint 1.3

questions.prompt: A colleague says “if you sampled correctly, the sample mean should equal the population mean exactly.” Is that true?
questions.answer: No. Only a census (sample = population) guarantees that. Any particular random sample gives a statistic (x̄) that usually differs from the parameter (μ) by sampling error, even when the sampling was done perfectly. Correct sampling makes the error unbiased and quantifiable (Chapters 6–7), not zero.

questions.prompt: Give a population and a sample for a study you might run as a Community Medicine resident, and name which of your numbers is the parameter and which the statistic.
questions.answer: Population: all pregnant women attending antenatal care in the district this year. Sample: the 200 women you interview. The true mean haemoglobin of all of them is the parameter (μ); the mean haemoglobin of your 200 women is the statistic (x̄).

questions.prompt: In the CBHI survey, 150 of 500 sampled households are members. Compute the membership proportion, give its symbol, and say whether it is a parameter or a statistic. Is the survey dataset primary or secondary data for a resident who reanalyses it five years later?
questions.answer: p̂ = 150 ÷ 500 = 0.30 (30%). It is computed from a sample, so it is a statistic, written p̂; it estimates the population proportion p (written π or P in some texts). For the original survey team the data were primary; for a resident reanalysing them later they are secondary data, collected by someone else for another purpose.
